channel.title: The Beholder's Gazette
channel.description: Your premier source for satirical news from across the realms. All the news that's fit to print (or burn).

item.title: Rogue Licks Glowing Ooze; Adventuring Party Now Lit Up
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A rogue licked glowing ooze on Undermaw Level Six to see what it was. His tongue now glows, and Brother Wendell says friends, please stop tasting walls.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, an adventuring party called the Lantern Pigs came up from Undermaw Level Six on Tuesday with a rogue whose tongue glows. Pip Nettlewhistle, a halfling, licked a patch of blue-green ooze on a dungeon wall "to check what it was." Eleven minutes later, his tongue began to shine through his cheek like a lantern behind a curtain.

The old herbals have a single rule on this, and it is a short one: never taste what you cannot name. A Brindlemoor Infirmary tally agrees, counting 19 wall-licking cases on the Undermaw ledger since spring, which is 19 more than I would like. Pip said the ooze "looked friendly." It was, in fairness, a gray ooze that had been leaning on a glow-moss colony, so the shine was only borrowed. The sting was not.

The trouble was how well the glow carried. Pip is the party's scout and sneaks for a living. Within the hour, three separate kobold ambush crews found the Lantern Pigs by following what they described as "a very rude blue tongue in the dark." Party cleric Sister Odda Marsh says Pip tried to whisper past a sentry with his mouth shut. His cheeks lit up and the sentry waved.

Sister Odda cast lesser restoration at the Level Four rest stop, which dimmed the tongue from a lantern to a candle. The rest, she says, has to wear off on its own, about four days. Pip may not scout until then, and for the duration he is to be known on the party roll as the Torch. He is said to be taking it well. He is also not taking sips of anything out of the water barrel.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the incident "a complimentary lighting upgrade" and said the guild had no plan to relabel the ooze. "We do not discourage tasting," he told this paper. "We discourage tasting without a permit." A permit costs eleven silver and, to be clear, covers no medical care.

You may recall that the Fourth Attempt drank nine unidentified potions last week, and one of them floats. A party that cannot keep its mouth shut is a healer's whole winter. So here is the rule, friends, as plain as a spoon: if it glows, you look at it. If it drips, you walk around it. If you have to ask a friend what it is, the friend should not be near it either.

For a tongue that has seen better days, I recommend a plain chicken-and-ginger broth, warm, not hot, with a slice of lemon to cut the memory of ooze. Three coppers, and no permit required. My friend Nyx tells me there is an app that identifies slime by photograph. Go outside, Nyx, and take a photograph of a tree.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Owlbear Union Vote at Hootline Ends 38 to 2, Sterling Rattled
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: The owlbear couriers at Hootline Couriers voted 38 to 2 to form a union on Monday. Sterling Vanmoor calls it a disruption of the workforce.
item.content:encoded:
The owlbear couriers at Hootline Couriers voted 38 to 2 on Monday to form a union, the first owlbear union in the history of the Brindlemoor exchange. The two holdouts were reportedly asleep. Founder and Chief Feather Officer Marla Quillfeather, whose firm was last week up 60% in its debut, called the result "a pivot toward stakeholder engagement." Her stock fell 11% by noon.

Let me say this plainly, friends: I do not love unions. I love growth. But I also love a good story, and this one has a lot of claws.

The union, styled the Amalgamated Order of Hooting Couriers, filed three demands with Chapter 9. Two goats per shift. An end to the mandatory company hat, which Hootline insists is a "brand halo" and the owlbears insist is a bucket. And a clause that parcels must be delivered "in whole, not in part," a reference to what organizers called "the Thursday situation."

Quillfeather held a press stand outside the Hootline warehouse on Tanner's Row. "Our owlbears are not employees," she said. "They are partners in a gig-based ecosystem." Behind her, an owlbear named Biscuit the shop steward ate her podium. I cannot confirm whether it was a negotiating tactic, but I would have called it one.

Rightsizing the adventuring party is a tool I defend. Rightsizing an owlbear is a tool I am told is called "a hand." Hootline's board has floated replacing the whole fleet with pigeons. Analyst Dunwick Harl of the Brindlemoor exchange noted pigeons carry only a twelfth of the payload, but "they do not have opinions." Within an hour, the pigeons had formed a committee of their own.

Some will say a 38 to 2 vote means management failed to listen. I say it means management found an extremely engaged workforce. When I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove at a gala in a hot-air balloon, he told me, "Sterling, a worker who bites is a worker who cares." I did not understand him then. I understand him now, and my left sleeve is shorter for it.

The owlbears have set a strike deadline of Friday. Until then, parcels continue to arrive, mostly. Reeve Fennick says the town is "aware of the owlbears" and has asked residents to leave goats on their porches as a goodwill measure. Several porches have since been entered.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Never put a hat on a workforce that can eat the hat.
  • A 38 to 2 vote is just a very large focus group.
  • Stock down 11% is a buying opportunity if you are very brave.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Wizard Casts Fireball in Tavern Back Room, Burns Own Party
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A wizard cast fireball in a 10-foot tavern back room on Fish Street during a brawl and the blast got his whole adventuring party. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the third bell after midnight, a wizard allegedly cast fireball inside a 10-foot-by-12-foot back room at the Leaking Boot on Fish Street, catching a card-table brawl and all four members of his own adventuring party, the Gilded Ladles. The Constabulary counted nine singed patrons, one melted card deck, and a cat that left through the ceiling.

'He said it would be fine,' said Dunstan Perrywick, a cooper, who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'He said the spell goes where you point it. Then he pointed it at the middle of the room, which is where the room was.' The turkey leg survived. Perrywick says this is the only part of the evening that went to plan.

The Ladles had gone into the back room to settle a bill dispute, and the brawl started when a rival table accused them of marking cards with a wand. Witnesses say the wizard, Orrin Tuck, shouted a warning. The cleric says it was 'everyone step back.' Tuck says it was 'everyone step in, I have a plan.' Nobody has produced the plan.

The blast filled the entire room, because that is what fireball allegedly does when the room is small. The fighter lost his eyebrows and half a cloak. The rogue lost her hat and, briefly, her faith in wizards. The cleric healed herself first, which the party is now calling 'a tactical decision' and which the fighter is calling something longer.

Keeper Dolly Ashgate says the fire also took the back-room door, a shelf of pickles, and 14 stools, for a total of 62 gold pieces in damage. 'Fire spread to the pickle shelf and the pickles screamed,' she said. 'I don't know why. I've never asked.' She has billed the party jointly. The party has asked who pays for a wizard's share. The Constabulary has said it is not a legal question, it is a seating chart.

Also, there was a lovely little silver spoon on the floor of the wreckage and I looked at it for a while. Anyway.

Tuck was found outside holding his hat, which was on fire. 'In my defense, the room was bigger in my head,' he said. Asked about the earlier Undermaw corridor fireball that also hurt his friends, Tuck said the two were 'unrelated, mostly.' The fighter, who is allegedly still smoking, asked this paper to print that the Ladles will vote on a new rule: no fireball indoors, no fireball in anything with a door, and no fireball if the cleric is holding a drink.

The Leaking Boot reopens Thursday with a new door and a sign reading 'FIREBALL: HALL ONLY.' The pickles are expected to recover. Allegedly.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Mimic Ballot Box Eats 31 Votes in Brindlemoor By-Election
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A mimic posing as the ballot box swallowed 31 ballots in a Brindlemoor Burgess by-election. The Council must now rule on whether the mimic voted.
item.content:encoded:
A mimic posing as the ballot box in Tuesday's Brindlemoor by-election swallowed 31 ballots before anyone noticed, the Returning Officer confirmed. The Burgess Council, which had only just recovered from the doppelganger who held two seats, has called a recess to discuss it.

The box had been in the Guildhall cellar since the last by-election, where it was labeled "Ballot Box (Oak)" and left unattended. Returning Officer Haldis Brume says she first grew suspicious when it asked for a second helping. "Ballot boxes are not supposed to say anything," she told the Chamber. "Certainly not 'more.'"

Procedure matters here, so I will state it. Under the Brindlemoor Charter, a ballot is valid once it is placed in the box. It is silent on what happens when the box places the voter in itself. Three voters were recovered, damp but willing to vote again. The other 28 ballots are, in the Returning Officer's words, "in the box, in a manner of speaking."

The gentleman from Tanner's Row moved that the 31 ballots be counted as cast, since the box had acted as a lawful receptacle. The lady from the Mill Ward moved that they be struck, since the box had acted as a lawful meal. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor, chairing, noted that she was "aware of the mimic" and asked both members to stop shouting at the furniture.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the box has been seen at four prior by-elections. "It always seemed heavy," the courtier said. "We assumed that was democracy."

The Council's tally for the session now stands at Promises Made, nine, and Promises Kept, none. The Chamber did pass a resolution to inspect all future furniture, which was drafted in two hours and vetoed by a chair. The chair was found to be a mimic as well. It has been removed, and the vote was retaken standing.

Two Burgesses have asked that the mimic be counted as a voter in its own right. Its ballot, they note, was the only one cast with total conviction. The Council's counsel advised that the Charter requires a voter to be a resident, a signatory, and, by the strictest reading, not a cellar. The ghost who filibustered for thirteen days offered to speak in the mimic's favor and was gently asked to sit.

For now the box sits in the Chamber, under guard, with a sign reading "Do Not Feed." Eleven Burgesses have already fed it a motion. The motion carried. Nobody read it.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Rope Trick Pod Launches at 90 gp; Exit Costs Extra
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: Cinderlatch's new 90 gp Rope Trick Pod opens an extradimensional room for eight hours. Nyx moved in for a weekend. Four eyes, and a landlord.
item.content:encoded:
OKAY. The Cinderlatch Rope Trick Pod is out in Brindlemoor shops today at 90 gp, and it is a rope trick you can carry in a satchel. Climb the rope, step into an extradimensional room for up to eight hours, and nobody can follow you in. I moved in for the weekend. I have notes!

The unboxing alone is worth the price. The pod is a brass cylinder with a rune-ring, a coil of enchanted rope, and a quick-start card that says 'Please do not read the other card.' I read the other card. It is the terms of service, and it is eleven feet long.

Setup took four minutes. The room itself is lovely: a cozy chamber, one cot, one lantern, no windows, and a mana throughput so smooth that my tea stayed hot for six hours. Runic latency on the rope was effectively zero. I pulled it up after me, exactly as promised, and for the first time in my life I was in a place where no one could ask me for a review.

Then the pod chimed. Hour seven brought a gentle notice: 'Your free hallway has expired.' It turns out the base 90 gp covers the room, and the way out is the Cinderlatch Egress tier at 4 sp a day. Without it, the rope retracts when the timer ends and you simply stand where the room used to be. Which is, I confirmed, a pantry in Cinderlatch's shipping office. Twice.

Byte, my pseudodragon, who now speaks only in ad copy, offered a review of his own. 'Upgrade to Egress Plus today,' he said, from inside the pod, where I had not invited him. I did not know he had been in there. He had been in there for the whole weekend. He has a cot now.

I asked Cinderlatch's launch spokesman, a smiling man named Dobb Wrenfield, whether charging for the exit was fair. 'It is not an exit,' he said. 'It is a premium egress experience.' Then he asked me to step away from the demo model, which I was still standing in.

My rival Brother Wendell Tumbleberry has already written that I should 'touch grass' instead of renting a pocket dimension. Wendell, the room has a lantern and no grass, and it is the best weekend I have had all year. You would hate it. Please do not buy one.

Verdict: the room is superb, the rope is smooth, the subscription is a crime, and I have already paid for the Egress tier. Four out of five beholder eyes. The fifth is locked behind Egress Plus.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Gold spent: 94. Pantries entered: 2. Familiars evicted: 0. Eyebrows: fine, for once.

item.title: Mimic Chest Opened Four Times After Party Splits Up
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Fourth Attempt split up to cover more ground on Level 6. All four corridors reached the same mimic chest, and all four members opened it alone.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 6 — The Fourth Attempt split up at a four-way junction yesterday to cover more ground, and all four of them ended up opening the same mimic. The chest, a handsome iron-banded thing in a dead-end room, was reached by each corridor in turn, and nobody was there to say what the last three had already learned.

The reasoning was sound on paper. The party's ranger, whose last navigational idea cost nine hours, proposed one corridor each, "to cover four times the ground." The fighter agreed. The wizard agreed. The party's bard, who asked to be named, agreed loudly, then went the wrong way on purpose to avoid the lecture.

The corridors were a loop. Chapter 9's map shows four branches and one room. I have the map. I rolled poorly and believed it.

The box score, in order of arrival: the ranger, first in at the ten-minute mark, found the chest and a note on its lid reading "Free." He opened it. Mimic. Ranger down to 7 hit points, and stuck. The wizard arrived twelve minutes later, saw a ranger-shaped lump in a chest, and cast detect magic on the ranger. The chest ate the wizard's spell focus. The wizard is at 4 hit points and has a sore wrist.

The fighter came third. "There was a chest, with two of my friends in it," he told me from a stretcher. "I thought, it's a trap, and I'm the one to deal with it." He is at 6 hit points. He died once before, and Shieldwall Mutual has already asked whether this counts as a second pre-existing condition. The bard arrived last, took one look, and sat on the floor and played a ballad. The mimic let him finish. Nobody has explained this, and I am not going to press it.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the party's hirelings, was waiting at the junction with the mule. He read the afternoon's clause aloud. "Splitting the party is permitted," he said. "Opening the same chest four times is a separate item." The hirelings, who took the one route that was not a loop, were unharmed and a day ahead on pay. The mule is, once again, at full health.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the map is "on track" and that the loop will be listed as a "scenic option" in the next printing. Chapter 9 has also confirmed that the chest is a monster, per its own hazard pay ruling, and that the party has no claim on the loot inside it. The loot inside it is the wizard's spell focus.

The ranger has asked to be released from the chest by the end of the week. Pottage says that is a negotiation. My ninth ten-foot pole of the season is still in there, too.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Adventuring Party Ambushes Envoy Carrying Their Reward
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: The Lantern & Lye Company ambushed a hooded rider at Quillmarch Bridge. He was Calimshan's envoy, carrying their 600 gp reward. Tension: three siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party ambushed a hooded rider on the road outside Quillmarch Bridge at dusk on Fifthday. The rider was the envoy of Calimshan, and he was carrying their 600 gold pieces in quest reward. The Lantern & Lye Company, a party of four, had been hired to clear a cellar of giant rats for the barony of Brackwater. They collected nothing for it until Fifthday, when they collected the envoy.

The facts are short. The envoy rode alone, hooded against the rain, and refused to stop when hailed. Refusing to stop is, by the party's own account, the first rule of being a villain. Their rogue dropped from a branch. Their wizard cast sleep, and the envoy's horse took it hardest. Their cleric asked questions only after the questions had stopped being useful.

"He had a hood," said the party's fighter, Dorrin Valecrest, outside the Brackwater magistrate's hall. "Nobody wears a hood in good faith. Also, he was carrying a very heavy bag, and it jingled." It was their pay. The bag was stamped with the Brackwater seal. The seal was the first clue anyone had looked at.

I interviewed the envoy from a safe distance. He sat on a bench with a blanket, one boot missing. He gave his name as Envoy Haskel Tharn. He expects an apology within the week. He declined to say whether he also expects the 600 gp, which the party has already counted twice and now insists is theirs.

This is where it turns into a siege. Brackwater says the party attacked a foreign diplomat on its soil. Calimshan says the party attacked a diplomat on a Brackwater road, which is a different thing and somehow worse. The party says they were paid late and did the arithmetic themselves. Tension stands at three siege-days. It was zero at breakfast.

Handshake review: the envoy and Dorrin Valecrest shook on a truce. Firm, one second, wet. Dagger detected, under the fighter's own cloak. It was returned to its owner.

A parley is scheduled at Quillmarch Bridge for Sixthday, where the bridge troll has already announced a toll for "armed company, and one horse that is not doing well." Brackwater will bring its magistrate. Calimshan will bring a lawyer and a fresh horse. The party will bring their invoice and, according to the cleric, a card.

I like an honest enemy. The party is not that. They are four people who ambushed their own paymaster and called it due diligence. Still, they were upfront about the part where they did it. The photo opportunity afterward, in which the party posed beside the envoy for a Brackwater clerk's sketch, I did not enjoy. I ate a field ration and watched the road.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Potion Testers Strike After Polymorph Batch Makes Newts of 9
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: Nine apprentice potion testers in Brindlemoor struck Monday after a polymorph batch turned them into newts for a day. They want hazard pay.
item.content:encoded:
Nine apprentice potion testers in Brindlemoor went on strike Monday. The reason is a polymorph batch that turned all of them into newts for most of Sunday.

The testers work at Dunmallow's Tinctures on Tanner's Row. Their job is to drink each new potion before it is sold and say what happens. Pay is 2 silver a vial. Nobody has ever written down what the pay is for if the answer is "I am a newt."

"I woke up on a lily pad in the cellar," said Wenna Thistlebrook, a taste-tester for three years. "I had no hands. I could not even write down my symptoms. That is a safety problem." She was a newt for fourteen hours. She says the worst part was the flies, which she found delicious, and which she wants it understood she does not approve of.

The shop calls the incident "an unplanned exploration of the amphibian wellness space." That means it turned nine workers into newts. Proprietor Hobb Dunmallow told reporters the batch was labeled "Mild Tonic, Possibly Cherry." He said the label was a draft.

The testers want three things. First, hazard pay of 6 silver a vial for any potion with no label. Second, a cleric on the premises who is awake. Third, a rule that a tester who becomes an animal is paid for the animal hours, because a newt is still on the clock, whatever else it is.

"They offered us a cheese plate," said Orrin Pellmere, a tester who spent Sunday as the cellar's second-largest newt. "Then they remembered we were newts and took it back. I want to be clear that I could have eaten the cheese."

Brindlemoor has watched this shop closely before. The pavement outside is still slightly purple from last spring. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor said her office is "aware of the newts" and has asked both sides to meet before Thursday. She said she hoped to avoid a second polymorph situation, though she conceded that this would depend on who is allowed to touch the vials.

The strike is forty-eight hours old and the shop has sold nothing. Customers who arrived Monday found a picket line of nine wet humans in blankets and one very small newt who would not say whether he was on strike or just lost. The testers have lent him a sign.

Dunmallow says he can hire replacements by Wednesday. The testers answer that every replacement will want to know what is in the vial. "That is the whole trouble," said Thistlebrook. "Somebody has to be the one who does not know."

A proper lunch break, a cleric who is awake, and pay for the newt hours. It is not much to ask. The guildmasters get a cloak for that.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Unidentified Ring Sold for 40 gp, Resold at 1,800 gp
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A party sold an unidentified ring of protection for 40 gp because nobody cast identify, then saw it priced at 1,800 gp. Barnaby has done the sums.
item.content:encoded:
The Hollow Lanterns, a four-member adventuring party out of the Undermaw, sold an unidentified ring to a Brindlemoor curio dealer on Monday for 40 gp. On Tuesday it was in his window as a ring of protection, priced at 1,800 gp. The difference is 1,760 gp, or 37,647 loaves on the current Loaf Index, which prices a loaf at 4.675 cp. (I have checked that. Four times.)

The ring came off a skeleton on Level Two. The party's wizard, Isolde Fernwhistle, owned a spell of identify but not the pearl it needs, which must be worth 100 gp and is consumed in the casting. A temple will cast it for a fee, but the temple was closed for a feast day. "We were tired and the ring was ugly," said Fernwhistle. "It was a little green. Nobody wanted to carry a green ring for a week."

The dealer, Odo Quillon, paid 40 gp, or 10 gp a head. That is 214 loaves each, which is a perfectly decent supper allowance for the week. Quillon cast identify that same afternoon, on the ring, with a pearl he buys by the dozen. He then priced it at what a ring of protection fetches in Brindlemoor, 1,800 gp, a figure that is 45 times what he paid. "I offered a fair price for what I was told it was," he said. "They told me it was a green ring."

Here is the arithmetic, and I would like everyone seated for it. Had the party waited a day and bought the pearl, they would have spent 100 gp, or 2,139 loaves, and held a ring worth 1,800 gp. After the pearl they would be 1,700 gp ahead of where they stand. Instead they are 40 gp up, and 1,760 gp behind the man who bought from them. Quillon's margin on one afternoon and one pearl, if the ring sells, is 1,660 gp. That is more than the Pellam Isles clerks I know earn in a year. (Four times.)

The Brindlemoor Adventurers' Guild, Chapter 9, says identification is "a personal responsibility" and that its standard form for selling loot says, in small print, "as seen." Fernwhistle has seen the form. She said she wishes she had seen it Monday. The party spent its 40 gp on a round at the tavern and a bandage, and returned to the shop Tuesday to look at the ring in the window. They did not go in. Fernwhistle reports they stood outside for eleven minutes. This is the same price pattern behind a potion of healing now costing 56 gp: the person who knows what a thing is always sells it for more than the person who found it.

My aunt Marigold keeps her savings in a boot, and the boot has never once been sold for less than it was worth, because everyone can see what a boot is. I used to laugh at her.

What this means for your pantry: a 100 gp pearl is 2,139 loaves, and an unidentified ring is a lottery ticket. Buy the pearl, or ask the temple, before you sell anything green.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Sleep Spell Drops 57 Brindlemoor Folk in the Extra Hour
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: A sleep spell cast to save the extra hour when Brindlemoor set its clocks back put 57 folk to sleep on their feet. Brother Wendell prescribes soup.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, a sleep spell cast to save the extra hour on the night Brindlemoor set its clocks back has put 57 townsfolk to sleep where they stood. The apprentice responsible, a lad named Ferrin Quill, told the Reeve's office he "only wanted a little extra rest for the town." The spell, as spells do, took it literally.

The clocks fell back at the second bell on Sunday morning, as they do every autumn, and Brindlemoor gained one hour it had not planned for. By the old herbals, an extra hour is a gift from the Harvest Mother. By Chapter 9, it is "an unlicensed hour," and the town's bell tower is still being scraped, so nobody was in a mood to argue.

Apprentice Quill reportedly cast sleep from the steps of the Sleeping Mule at about the stroke of the repeated hour. The spell was meant for one pillow. It caught a cooper, three choir boys, a mule, and a visiting cleric who was, witnesses say, halfway through a sermon on the virtues of wakefulness. He finished the sentence in his sleep.

"I found three of them stacked by the door like firewood," said Hilde, a turnip farmer. "One was snoring in rhyme." The Sleeping Mule has since put a sign on its cellar door asking sleepers not to nap on the barrels.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick said Chapter 9 regards the incident as "a scheduled rest, recently unscheduled." He added that Level Seven of the Undermaw will open next tenday. Nobody laughed, because everyone was asleep or nearly so.

Now for the science, friends. The old herbals say a tired body mends best on a full night's sleep, and the temple studies agree: adults who sleep seven to nine hours catch fewer colds and cough less. The magic kind of sleep, however, does not count. Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor of Chapter 9 confirmed that the sleepers woke feeling "exactly as tired as before," which is the trouble with borrowed rest. It leaves you nothing to give back.

The 57 were all awake by the following noon, with only a stiff neck apiece and, in the cooper's case, a barrel-shaped crease on his face. Shieldwall Mutual says napping is covered, but only the voluntary kind.

So here is my advice. Go to bed at your usual hour, spend the extra one honestly, and leave the spellbook shut. Barley and mushroom soup, thick with thyme, is the proper nightcap. I would suggest my friend Nyx try it too, though first Nyx should go outside and see a morning that came by itself.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Adventuring Party Haggles an Hour, Pays 8 gp Over Sticker
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: An adventuring party haggled an hour over 3 silver on a potion of healing and paid 58 gp, 7 sp against a 50 gp sticker. Sterling Vanmoor is inspired.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party called the Salt Road Six spent a full hour haggling over 3 silver on a single potion of healing in Brindlemoor on Saturday, and walked out paying 58 gp, 7 sp against a posted price of 50 gp. The shop is Halsk's Curios and Cordials on Tanner's Row. Its owner, Dorrin Halsk, calls the result "a deal both sides can feel something about."

Some people see eight and a half extra gold pieces. I see the best-executed customer journey of the quarter. The Salt Road Six came in with a plan, a rogue who "reads people," and a bard who offered to pay in exposure. Halsk opened with a firm 50 gp. The party countered at 49 gp, 7 sp. Forty minutes of eye contact followed.

Here is where the pivot happened. Halsk, a true thought-leader in retail, introduced a negotiation consultation fee of 1 gp per quarter hour, billed to whoever spoke first. Then came the candle surcharge (2 gp, because haggling "burns light"), the chair fee (3 sp each, six chairs), and mule parking at 4 gp, which the party's mule had not asked for and could not refuse. By the time the rogue said "fine, fifty," the sticker price was a fond memory.

"We saved three silver on the potion," said the party's rogue, Hesper Moult, holding her receipt. "It says so right here, under the line that says 'Rogue's Discount Applied, Then Reversed.'" Her bard, asked whether the hour was worth it, said the experience had been "a journey."

Shieldwall Mutual has declined to comment, though a clerk confirmed the policy excludes any loss the party was warned about, including the chair fee. The Salt Road Six plan to haggle again next week, this time at a rival shop. Halsk says he will welcome them with open arms and a fresh price list.

I met a retired guildmaster of the Copper Exchange at a gala once, and he told me, "Sterling, the customer who haggles has already agreed to pay. All that's left is the amount." I think about that every day. I also think about it whenever I see a mule.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

  • Never haggle in a chair you haven't priced.
  • If the shopkeeper smiles, you are already the product.
  • A discount that is later reversed is just a loyalty program.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Owlbear Naps in Laundry Cart; Fish Street Waits 2 Days
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: An owlbear fell asleep in a laundry cart on Fish Street and has not moved in two days. The Constabulary says nobody is waking it. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after midnight on Sunday, an owlbear climbed into a laundry cart on Fish Street, curled up on 61 households' worth of clean sheets, and went to sleep. Two days later it is still there, and the Constabulary has declined to wake it. Allegedly this is policy.

'We are monitoring the situation,' said Constabulary Sergeant Brom Teasel, who was monitoring it from the far side of a pie stall. 'It snores. The snore has a beak in it. We have put up 14 rope posts and a sign that says Please Do Not.' The sign was allegedly chewed by lunchtime. The rope posts are fine. The posts are not the problem.

The sheets belong to Pim Oddlow, a laundress, who says the cart held every bedsheet on the east side of the street, freshly pressed. 'Sixty-one households,' she said, wringing a towel at the time. 'Sixty-one beds with nothing on them. The owlbear has not paid for the starch.' Oddlow estimates the loss at 38 gold, plus whatever the owlbear is doing to the pillowcases, which she described only as 'nesting.'

Neighbors have organized. Corvin Stubb, a baker, was holding a tray of rolls when he told me the street is 'quiet for the first time in years,' and that business is up because gawkers buy snacks. A rival baker on the other side of the road reported the opposite. A third man, who gave his name only as Dobbin and was eating a turkey leg, said he is fine with the owlbear but wants it known that he saw the cart first. Nobody asked him.

Also there is a really nice brass lantern hook two doors down, just sitting there, very shiny. Anyway. Recovered.

The Tower District has weighed in. A nobles' committee, speaking from a safe distance of eleven miles, called the situation 'a failure of Lower City sanitation' and asked that the owlbear be moved somewhere less visible. Fish Street's answer was to hang the committee's letter on the rope posts as decoration. Skritch is told the owlbear has not read it. Skritch is also told that pigeons have started roosting on its back, which is the single worst development of the week.

Sergeant Teasel says the Constabulary will act when the owlbear wakes on its own, or when the sheets need to be returned, whichever comes later. He has asked the public not to throw anything at it, not to sing to it, and not to try to borrow a pillowcase. Three people have reportedly tried to borrow a pillowcase. One of them is Dobbin.

For now, Fish Street runs on tiptoe, and the laundry cart rolls nowhere. The Constabulary says the matter is under control. Allegedly.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Adventuring Party Votes Six Hours on Two Dungeon Doors
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: An adventuring party on Level Three of the Undermaw spent six hours voting on which of two doors to open, and finished in the dark.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party called the Copper Candle Company spent six hours on Level Three of the Undermaw on Saturday voting on which of two dungeon doors to open. By the time they reached a result, all six of their torches had burned out, which the minutes record as 'a matter for the next session.'

The trouble began when Dunstan Mirelle, a dwarf cleric, rose to move that the party 'consider the door on the left.' The gentleman from the rear guard, a halfling archer, seconded it and immediately offered an amendment to consider the door on the right instead. A point of order followed on whether an amendment may undo the motion it amends. The party's wizard held that it may. The party's fighter held that she was hungry.

The first vote split two to two, with the rogue abstaining on the grounds that doors were 'a conflict of interest.' She has picked locks professionally for eleven years. A recount was requested and granted. It also came out two to two, though the minutes note that one member voted twice in a spirit of enthusiasm.

Three amendments then reached the floor. One proposed opening the left door but with a rope. One proposed opening neither and having a snack. The third, from the wizard, proposed forming a subcommittee of one to examine the doors, which would have been the wizard. It was ruled out of order by the chair, who was also the wizard's brother-in-law.

By my count the party made nine procedural promises during the evening, including 'we will be brief,' and kept the one about adjourning, though not on time. The torch situation was raised at hour three. A motion to light a seventh torch failed because the party had packed six. The motion carried, in the sense that nobody opposed it, but it did not produce a torch. Nobody read it.

A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake told me the doors were 'the least interesting thing in that corridor.' He was right. At the sixth hour, a wandering skeleton from behind the left door knocked politely and asked whether the party intended to use the passage, as it had been waiting since supper. The party moved to table the question. The skeleton seconded.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the guild 'has every confidence in the party's process' and that delve permits do not specify how doors are chosen. 'We are aware of the voting,' he said. 'It is on track.' Reeve Fennick declined comment, having recently sat through thirteen days of a ghost.

The Copper Candle Company has scheduled a follow-up session for Saturday. The agenda lists one item: the door on the right, subject to amendment.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Alarm Spell Wakes Party 14 Times During One Long Rest
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: The Mudsock Vanguard cast Alarm around camp for a safe long rest. Squirrels, a moth, and their own rogue woke them 14 times. Nyx loved it. Byte did not.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's Mudsock Vanguard cast the Alarm spell around their camp on the Undermaw's second landing this week, hoping for one uninterrupted long rest. They got fourteen interruptions instead. I have been reviewing the ward ever since, because I am a professional and also because I couldn't sleep either!

Here is the log, as read back by the party's wizard, Pennick Thrallowby. The first four alerts were squirrels. The fifth was a moth. Pennick says it was "a very small moth," and Alarm, which has no concept of small, rang the mental chime at full volume. Alerts six through nine were more squirrels, possibly the same squirrel, who appears to have started charging the perimeter for sport. Alerts ten, eleven, twelve and fourteen were the party's own rogue, Dessa Quillfoot, walking out of the ward to pee and walking back in.

"I whispered that I was going out," Dessa said. "The ward doesn't care that I whispered. It cares that I crossed it. Four times. Nobody warned me about the bladder tax."

The runic latency is outstanding. Alert thirteen, which was a genuine owlbear-sized shape at the edge of the clearing, arrived in under a second, and I would like that on the box. It turned out to be a cart. The cart was empty. Nobody could tell me why a cart was in a clearing in the Undermaw, and nobody had the strength to ask.

The core problem is mana throughput. Alarm sounds in the caster's head only, so Pennick took every alert alone while the rest of the party snored. By dawn the cleric had her prayers back, the fighter had his hit dice, and the wizard had a twitch. A long rest needs eight hours with no more than two of strenuous activity, and the Guild's own pamphlet says so. Chapter 9 declined to comment on whether a rogue's bathroom schedule counts as strenuous.

My familiar Byte, who sat through the entire demo, said "Alarm. Because you deserve to wake up." He then bit the moth. I assume that is a ruling.

Pennick has since switched to a different method, which is sleeping in shifts and trusting the dog. He also asked me to note that he is "not mad, just thin." Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to touch grass, but the grass is where the squirrels live, Wendell.

Four out of five beholder eyes. The ward works exactly as written, and that is the whole problem.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

Damage Report: Alerts sustained: 14. Squirrels: 9 (or 1). Moths bitten: 1. Spell slots recovered: 0. Eyebrows: fine, but I am very tired.

item.title: Rust Monster Lured Off Level Seven Step With Nail Trail
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: Chapter 9 coaxed the sleeping rust monster off Level Seven's top step with a trail of nails and declared the level open. The trail went down, not out.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 7 LANDING — A rust monster that has slept on the top step of Level Seven for two weeks was lured away at dawn with a trail of 340 iron nails, and Chapter 9 declared the level open for the first time in three years. I was there. I rolled poorly on the timing, standing on the step when the monster woke, and I am now missing one belt buckle.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick laid the nails himself, one every foot, from the sleeper's nose down the stairwell. "Everything is on track," he told the crowd of ticket-holders, who had paid four copper to watch the animal nap and were not sure what they were owed now that it was awake. The monster ate its way down the steps with the unhurried manner of a patron at a good buffet. It did not look back.

Chapter 9 then cut a new ribbon with wooden shears, a lesson from the ticket-sales fortnight. The Fourth Attempt went through first. Their tally: fighter at 14 hit points, wizard at 11, ranger at 12, and the party's bard, who asked to be named, at "a lot of feelings." The hirelings were not asked to hold the door. I count that as a win for the profession.

The trouble came at the bottom of Level Seven, where the nail trail did not stop. Steward Ansel Pottage of the hirelings, who reads every document to the end and every floor the same way, noted that the nails ran straight into a stairwell nobody had mapped. "The contract says Level Seven," he said. "It does not say what is under it." The monster is now asleep on the top step of Level Eight, which Chapter 9's maps describe as "not yet a level."

Oddingwick called the development "soft downward growth." Chapter 9 intends to sell tickets to the new step, pending a hearing. Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor, who will chair it, asked only whether the nails were reimbursable, since she has seen the invoice.

Ten-foot poles lost this season: eleven. The twelfth went down the stairwell with the monster, which ate the iron tip and left the shaft as a courtesy. Every adventurer on the landing agreed it was the first thing the level has done for us.

A footnote on the map: Chapter 9's Level Seven sheet is reissued today as accurate. It shows a staircase going down. That much, at least, is true.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Bard's Lie at Border Checkpoint Costs Party Far Over 2 Copper
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: An adventuring party's bard lied to a Brackwater guard who only wanted a 2-copper toll. It is now a diplomatic incident, at eleven siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party called the Lanternlit Five spent Fifthday turning a 2-copper toll at Dunwick Gate, the Brackwater border post, into a diplomatic incident. Their bard, Pip Lutewhistle, told the guard on duty that the party was escorting a royal wedding. No such wedding exists. Tension between Brackwater and Ashenfold now stands at eleven siege-days.

The facts are short. Sergeant Ottwin Marsh asked for two copper pieces. The party's fighter reached for her purse. Lutewhistle stepped in front of her and began to talk.

He said the party served the Grand Duchess of Velmora-by-the-Sea, a realm that appears on no map. He said the mule, draped in a veil after a casting of disguise self, was the bride. He said the groom was delayed by a minor war. Marsh wrote this down, because writing things down is what a sergeant does when he cannot think of a response.

"I asked for two copper," Marsh told this correspondent. "He gave me a kingdom. I did not have a form for a kingdom."

The lie did what lies do under pressure: it grew. Lutewhistle added a dowry of nine hundred goats and a treaty clause. He added a rival suitor from Ashenfold, which was the mistake. Marsh, a loyal Brackwater man, sent a runner to the barony's envoy, Teodra Hallowmere.

Hallowmere arrived within the hour and shook the bard's hand. Firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected, though a lute pick was found in the sleeve. She then did what she does best and taxed the intent. The party owes two copper for the toll, nine silver for the unlicensed dowry, and an undisclosed sum for the goats, which do not exist but are, in her words, "legally implied."

Ashenfold has denied having a suitor, a rival, or a position on the mule. Its envoy, Halric Dunmere, called the accusation "a provocation wrapped in a veil." Both baronies have moved a cart across the road. Nobody has moved it back.

The Lanternlit Five are being held at the post in the guard's own tent, where the cook is feeding them well. Field rations, mostly. The party's fighter, who asked not to be named, said she had the two copper in her hand the entire time. "I had it out," she said. "Out. In my palm."

Lutewhistle says he regrets nothing and is already drafting a ballad. Marsh says the ballad had better rhyme with "toll." The party will be released once the wedding is cancelled, which requires a wedding.

Nobody won today. The mule is still wearing the veil.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Loot Split Dispute: Torchbearer Paid in 'Exposure'
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: An adventuring party split a 4,200 gold hoard five ways and paid its hired torchbearer in exposure. She filed a grievance with Chapter 9 on Monday.
item.content:encoded:
Pay the torchbearer. Wenna Tarrowby, a halfling hireling, filed a grievance with Chapter 9 on Monday after an adventuring party called the Silver Thistle Company split a 4,200 gold hoard five ways and gave her nothing but exposure. Eleven hours underground. One eyebrow gone. Her cut of the loot split came to a mention in a ballad.

The Thistles are five: a fighter, a wizard, a cleric, a rogue and a bard. The bard wrote the ballad. 'Exposure' is how the party's own paperwork describes the pay. Translated: nothing. Eight hundred and forty gold each for the five of them, and for the woman who held the light, a chorus.

'I carried the torch, the spare torch, and the spare spare torch,' said Tarrowby, a torchbearer for six years. 'The wizard asked me to hold his hat. I held the hat. In the ballad I am called "a faithful flicker." I am five foot nothing and I have never flickered.'

The Thistles say it was a misunderstanding. 'We offered her tremendous visibility,' said Corrin Vexlow, the bard, who is also the party's treasurer, which is the first mistake. 'Half of Brindlemoor will know her name by Fifthday. You can't buy that.' Tarrowby says you can, in fact, buy it, and the price is 840 gold, the same as everyone else's.

It gets worse. The hoard included a chest of 600 gold the party found because Tarrowby's torch lit a pressure plate. She stepped around it. They did not thank her. The wizard then used the chest as a footstool for the walk home.

Ansel Pottage, steward of hirelings, was reading the Thistles' contract aloud outside Chapter 9 by midmorning, all the way to the end, which is more than the Thistles had done. 'Clause nine,' he said. 'Hirelings receive a share. Clause nine does not say what kind.' He then paused for the crowd. 'It does say "in coin."' The crowd, about forty hirelings with their own torches, cheered. Pottage was careful to add that the clause is in the party's own handwriting.

The hearing goes to Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor, who has ruled on hireling pay before and was last seen carrying a ladle. Deputy Registrar Oddingwick called the dispute 'a soft launch of a compensation conversation' and said the guild is 'on track.' Nobody knows what track.

Here is the plain version. A half share is the going rate for hirelings in the Undermaw. That is 420 gold. A ballad is not coin. Neither is a mention, or a hat held. When a party says 'exposure,' it means they spent the money. The torchbearer was the only one who could see where she was going, and she is the one who went home with nothing.

The Thistles have offered Tarrowby a second verse. She has asked for a second share.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Healing Potion Price Up 12% to 56 gp as Delves Surge
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A potion of healing now costs 56 gp in Brindlemoor, up 12% from 50 gp, as more parties enter the Undermaw. Barnaby has checked the loaves. Twice.
item.content:encoded:
The price of a potion of healing in Brindlemoor rose 12% on Monday, from 50 gp to 56 gp, as Chapter 9 reported a 31% jump in delve permits for the month. Apothecaries on Tanner's Row blame demand from the Undermaw. I blame arithmetic. (I have checked this four times.)

Six gold pieces sounds small until you do the Loaf Index. At 4.675 cp a loaf, a 50 gp potion was worth about 1,070 loaves. At 56 gp it is worth about 1,198. That is 128 extra loaves per potion, which is a loaf-bearing cart of bread, standing still, in a cellar, because of a cut finger on Level Four.

The mechanism is old and boring, which is the nice thing about it. More parties go down. More parties come up needing mending. Apothecaries make potions at roughly the same speed as last month, because the herb gatherers are fixed in number and the alchemists refuse to hurry. When buyers rise and supply doesn't, the price must go somewhere, and it went up. Nobody is cheating. A shortage is just a queue with a price tag.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 called the permit surge "entirely on track" and said the guild would welcome the new revenue. Asked whether the guild intended to help with potions, he said the guild intended to help with permits. Reeve Fennick said only that the town was aware of the price.

Shieldwall Mutual has already adjusted its premiums. A spokesman said a potion is now classed as "a small asset" and an adventurer who drinks one without a receipt is "a claim waiting to happen." The Fourth Attempt reportedly bought nine potions last week, then drank four of them on the walk to the entrance, which a Pettibone & Vail clerk called "a very expensive warm-up."

Some will say the market will fix this by itself, and that new alchemists will rush in. (Sterling Vanmoor said so on Sunday, smiling.) I would only note that an alchemist takes six years to train and a delve permit takes six minutes. Prices will climb faster than the apprentices.

My aunt Marigold, who keeps her savings in a boot, tells me she has not bought a potion since the Third Attempt, and that she heals by sitting down. I used to think this was foolish. Her boot has not risen 12% in anything.

What this means for your pantry: buy your bread now, buy your bandages now, and do not enter the Undermaw if you can help it. If you must, pack a roll of linen. It costs a single loaf.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Party Drinks 9 Unidentified Potions; One Now Floats
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: The Fourth Attempt drank all nine unidentified potions from an Undermaw haul to see what they did. The infirmary has results. Soup is advised.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the temple infirmary on Tanner's Row has admitted four members of the Fourth Attempt after the party drank nine unidentified potions from a Level Six haul, on Saturday evening, "to see what they do." The potion mix-up is now in its second day. The healers say the party will recover. They also say it is a good deal of work for a Sunday.

Here is the ledger as I have it. The party's rogue is invisible and has been since Saturday night. Healers know she is in bed six only because the blanket is dented. The cleric has been floating about a foot above his cot since supper, and a nurse ties his ankle to the bedpost each night so he does not drift into the rafters. The fighter drank something that made him eight inches tall, and is being kept in a soup bowl, which he says is "not as funny as it sounds." The wizard, who drank the most, will speak only to fish. The infirmary has lent him a tank of carp, and he is, by every account, getting on well with them.

Ansel Pottage, the party's steward, was the only one who did not drink. "I read the vials," he said, bandaged as ever. "Three had labels. Nobody asked me about the other six." He added that the party's contract does not cover "voluntary tasting," and that he has read the clause aloud twice.

Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick of Chapter 9 said the haul was "on track" and that the potions were "enthusiastically sampled." Asked whether the guild would require labels on loot, he said a labeling desk is "in early discussion." Shieldwall Mutual says it does not cover the floating, the shrinking, or the fish, which it files under "your own fault."

Now for the advice, friends. The old herbals say never swallow a strange brew, and the old herbals have never been wrong about this. As for the newer studies, the Marrowfield apothecaries now make every potion of healing list its side effects, and the finding is simple: an unmarked vial is a gamble with your own insides. If you must test, test one potion at a time. Do it with a healer in the room, a full night's rest ahead of you, and a pot on the stove. Nine at once leaves nobody able to say which one made the knees go strange.

Better still, take the unknown vials to an honest herbalist, or a friendly sage with a good nose and a magnifying glass. A sage charges less than a night in the infirmary, and the carp are not cheap to feed. My friend Nyx tells me there is a spell for identifying things now. Go outside, Nyx, and try it on a pebble.

The rogue, when last seen, was sitting up and sipping broth. The healers can tell because the spoon keeps going down. For the fighter and the rest I recommend clear onion broth with a little ginger: easy on the stomach and gentle on the nerves. It also goes well with carp, if the wizard will let you.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Fighter Kicks Unlocked Tavern Door; Party Billed 17 Gold
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: An adventuring party was billed 17 gold and 5 silver after their fighter kicked in a Brindlemoor tavern door that was unlocked. The rogue made it worse.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after sundown, an adventuring party was allegedly billed 17 gold and 5 silver at the Crooked Latch tavern on Tanner's Row in Brindlemoor. The reason: their fighter kicked in the front door, and the front door was unlocked. It had been unlocked, per the innkeeper, since the Feast of the Thaw, and the sign on it said PULL.

'He backed up,' said Dellin Marrowick, a cooper who was eating a turkey leg at the time. 'He took a real run at it. Three steps, a shout, and the whole door came off its hinges and slid into the soup.' The fighter, a dwarf named Torgan Ironquay, allegedly said, 'It was stuck.' The door was not stuck. It was a door.

Keeper Hobb Pennywhistle presented the party with an itemized bill before the soup had stopped moving. One door, oak, 4 gold. Two hinges, 1 gold. One sign (PULL), now in pieces, 5 silver. 'I don't charge for the shouting,' Pennywhistle told this reporter. 'That was a courtesy.'

This is where the party's rogue, a halfling called Wimble Thistlebrook, stepped in. 'Hold on,' she said. 'Nobody touch that. I'm going to check it for traps.' She then spent what witnesses put at forty minutes examining a door that was lying flat on the floor. She tapped it with a ten-foot pole. She sprinkled flour over it. She listened to it. At one point she allegedly asked the door whether it was trapped, and waited.

The flour was Pennywhistle's flour. That was 8 silver. The ten-foot pole went through the ceiling, which was 3 gold, and knocked down a bell that, the Keeper says, 'was the only trap in the building, and it was for rats.' The bell was 2 gold. Wimble, to her credit, found it. 'I disarmed it,' she said. 'Eventually.' Also there was a really nice brass hinge pin rolling around under table six. Anyway.

Torgan has asked that the record show the door 'looked locked.' Reeve Fennick's office, reached for comment, said the town is 'aware of the door' and has no plans to rule on whether a door can look locked. Chapter 9 of the Adventurers' Guild confirmed that no permit is needed to kick a door, but a permit is needed to kick a door 'with intent.' Deputy Registrar Oddingwick called the incident 'a soft opening of the Crooked Latch's second entrance.'

The party paid in full, plus a tip, since the fighter allegedly felt bad. The Fourth Attempt, who were seated at table two throughout, declined to comment but were seen quietly checking their own doors.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)
